prompt:
The rain came off the bay all morning, and Fiona Doyle arrived at the Fenwick Street loading door with her collar turned up and four cardboard boxes in the back of a borrowed station wagon.
Nadia met her under the concrete awning with a trolley and a sheet of plastic. The archive occupied the basement of the old Carnegie library, and its smell climbed the steps to meet them: wet stone, cold paper, the chemical breath of the dehumidifiers that ran day and night.

Gus nodded slowly and did not look at the boxes again. Nadia noticed that. She noticed most things twice.
The work took the afternoon. She wore cotton gloves and used a soft pencil and acid-free folders, sorting by year, by hand, by the smell of the paper. Cormac Doyle had kept everything. Tide tables annotated in three colors. Receipts for fuel and rope and a new bilge pump. A notebook of weather, wind and swell and visibility, going back to the nineties.

Gus left at a quarter past five, and paused in the doorway with his coat over his arm. "Lock the front when you go," he said. "And the back. The alarm's been temperamental." "I know," Nadia said. "Set it twice if it argues." He held out the tin of licorice, then put it away when she shook her head. The outside door banged. The rain went on without him.
She waited until the building had settled into its evening quiet, until the last footsteps crossed the floor above and the library lights went off in rows. Then she unlocked the lower drawer of her desk and lifted out the biscuit tin.

Then a second voice, close to the microphone, calm and unhurried. "This channel is closed. You will not repeat what you heard tonight. You will go home and forget the whole night." A pause. "Do you understand me?" Nadia's finger found the stop button, but she did not press it. She sat with the headphones warm on her ears and let the tape run.
And then Emeka spoke. It was a whisper. "Nadia." He said her name the way he always had, the middle syllable long. "Don't look for me. I'm all right. Look at the water. Do you hear me? Look at the water."

She was reaching for the volume when the light changed in the frosted window of the door. Gus stood there with his coat still on and his keys in his hand. He had come back for something and had not expected the back room to be lit. He pushed the door open and looked at the machine, then at her, and his face did a thing she had never seen it do.
"Where did you get that?" "It was in Cormac Doyle's boxes. Gus, listen—"

The house on Salt Row had been her grandmother's, narrow and gray and set into the hill with its face to the water. Nadia parked the Volvo at the curb and sat a moment with the engine off, listening to the rain on the roof. The tape deck had been broken for four years. The radio worked, but she rarely turned it on.
Inside, she put the kettle on and went to the back of the closet, where the box had sat through two moves and one divorce. It held what she had kept from 2014: newspaper clippings gone yellow at the edges, a folded program from the memorial service, a photocopy of the police case file that a clerk should not have given her.

"You look tired," her mother said.
"I've been sleeping badly."
"You always sleep badly." Adaeze sat across from her, hands folded, and waited.

The harbor authority's records had come to the archive on permanent loan decades ago, and nobody had asked for them since. Nadia found the KSTL binders on the bottom shelf of the far stack, where the ceiling leaked and Gus kept a plastic tub to catch the drips. Three grey lever-arch files, spines faded to the color of dishwater, each holding one year of the station's operating log.
She carried the 2014 binder to the listening desk under the fluorescent tube that flickered and never quite died, and opened it. The log was a form. Every hour the engineer on duty initialed a line and noted transmitter power, modulation, weather. Most of the year was Gus's handwriting, small and upright, and seeing it there was like hearing a voice through a wall.

She turned back a page, then forward, and checked the whole week. The handwriting after 3 March was not Gus's. It was rounder, more careful, the sort of hand taught to make its letters touch the line. She had seen it before, on the reel label, on the box of clippings she had carried down from her grandmother's attic, on a birthday card from 2013.
She closed the binder and held both palms flat on the cover until her breathing evened out.

She went on a Saturday, early, before the archive opened. The coast road north out of Marrow Bay climbed through wet spruce and ran along the top of the cliffs, and the Volvo's wipers beat a slow argument with the rain. Salt fogged the windshield faster than the defroster could clear it. She drove with both hands and hummed, very quietly, a tune she did not know she knew.
Kestrel Point was a knuckle of black rock with a stand of wind-bent pines behind it, and the station sat on the crown of it like something left behind by a tide. One mast, guy-wired, leaning. A low cinderblock building with a flat roof, a chain-link fence gone orange with rust. The sign by the gate still said KSTL 1140 in letters faded to the color of old newspaper.

She crouched and swept the light along the wall, and the beam caught the edge of a panel that did not sit flush with the others. She got her fingers behind it. It came away with a sound of old screws giving up, and behind it, in the cavity between the studs, lay a logbook.
It was a duplicate working log, cloth-bound, swollen with damp, the pages ruled in blue. She opened it on the bench and turned to March. The entries were in several hands and one of them she knew. Every hour of the night of the third was there, carrier on, power steady, storm static heavy, mast holding, and in the margin beside the last entry, in pencil, a single word: kept.

He came on a Tuesday, in the afternoon, when the archive was empty except for Nadia and Gus and the hum of the dehumidifier. The rain had stopped and the light through the high basement windows was the color of weak tea. He knocked on the open door instead of walking in, which she noticed.
Desmond Rusk was forty-five and looked it in the way of men who pay attention. Grey at the temples, a good dark coat, shoes that had never been in weather. He carried no umbrella and was not wet, which meant he had come from a car at the curb. He introduced himself with a card held between two fingers and said he hoped he was not interrupting. His voice was low and unhurried, and he used her name often, the way a man does when he wants it remembered that he has taken the trouble to learn it.

"Those records are public," Nadia said. "Anyone can read them here. There's a table and a lamp and a pencil cup."
Rusk smiled. It was a good smile, well made, and it did not reach the middle of his face. "Public is not the same as safe," he said. "Basements flood. I'm sure you know about the leak in the far stack."

Rain came sideways off the bay all afternoon, striking the archive's high windows in long gray sheets. Nadia heard Fiona Doyle on the stairs before she saw her: boots, a coat shaken out, water scattering across the linoleum. Fiona came down carrying a canvas bag and the smell of the harbor, salt and diesel and cold weed.
She was twenty-nine and looked younger when she was angry, which was most of the time now. Her father had been dead three weeks and she had not yet found a use for her hands. Nadia cleared the second chair and set the reel on the worktable between them, in its cardboard box, the label in handwriting she still could not say aloud. KSTL 3/3/14, weather log.

On the screen the storm was a solid gray band. She put a high-pass filter across it, notched out the mains hum, then ran a second pass to cut the hiss that lives above eight kilohertz like a thin continuous rain. The waveform thinned. Shapes began to show.
"There," Fiona said. A cluster of peaks beneath the wind, near the eleventh minute. Nadia looped it, slowed it, cleaned it again, and the voice came up out of the noise warped but unmistakable, a man speaking close to a microphone with the flat patience of someone used to being obeyed.

The Marrow Bay police station sat on Harbor Street behind a stand of wind-bent spruce, its windows steamed and its gutters running. Nadia waited forty minutes in a room with plastic chairs and a framed photograph of a ferry that no longer ran, listening to the fluorescent tubes tick and the rain drum on the flat roof above her.
Detective Joaquin Serrano came down at last, a paper cup in one hand and a folder he did not seem to want under his arm. He was fifty-two, gray at the temples, wearing a cardigan under a jacket that had given up on him years ago. His eyes were the eyes of a man who slept in pieces. "Ms. Okonkwo," he said. "You called about a tape."

"Cormac Doyle's papers. His daughter donated them to the archive." Nadia kept her voice even. "The original is in the archive. Unlogged. It came in a biscuit tin."
He turned the paper cup a quarter turn, then back. "The Doyle file was thin," he said at last. "Three pages of narrative and a coroner's finding. I remember thinking it was thin even for a drowning." He breathed out through his nose. "When I pulled it again in 2019 there were pages missing from the evidence log. Signatures that went nowhere. Photographs referenced and not present. I filed a note and the note came back to me with nothing on it."

The rain stopped overnight and left the morning gray and low, the clouds sitting on the rooftops like a lid. The archive smelled of wet stone and the boiler, which clanked and sighed in its corner as if it were the only thing in the building with opinions. Nadia came in early, before Gus, and turned on the long row of fluorescents one bank at a time.
The harbor authority's records were on permanent loan and filled forty boxes in the north stacks, ledgers and manifests and inspection slips going back to the fifties. She had spent a week of lunch hours among them already. Now she pulled the shipping ledgers for 2013 and 2014 and laid them open on the worktable, and beside them she set the engineer's logbook from Kestrel Point, its pages soft as cloth.

Then she found the casualty list, misfiled in a folder of crew agreements. Tobias Renn, deckhand, aged twenty-three, died aboard. The cause of death was given as accidental. There was no inquest, no witness statement, no name of the officer who had signed the entry. The handwriting was the same as the handwriting on the four-line sinking report.
She sat back and listened to the boiler for a while. The fluorescent light hummed at the edge of hearing, the note she had trained herself years ago to ignore.

The rain had been at it since before dawn, and the basement door of the Carnegie library stood open an inch when Nadia came down Fenwick Street with her key already in her hand. She knew before she touched it. Eleven years of cataloguing had taught her the sound of a thing out of place.
She went in sideways and found the lights. The fluorescents stuttered and held, and she could see the damage from the end of the stacks: her office door open, the desk drawers pulled and dropped, the filing boxes dumped into a drift of paper. Somebody had searched with a methodical anger, the way a person does when they already know what they are looking for.

The police came and took photographs and a statement and were gone inside an hour. Nothing else was missing. Not the petty cash, not the computers, not the harbor authority ledgers on permanent loan. Only the reel, and the report that said it did not exist.
That afternoon the complaint arrived. Gus brought it to her desk on a single sheet of letterhead, holding it by the corner as though it were wet. Rusk Marine Holdings alleged that a municipal employee had been removing and mishandling records on permanent loan, and requested a review of the archive's staffing. The city would decide within the week whether her position, which was not permanent, would continue.

She asked him the question sideways, the way you approach a damaged tape. "Gus. In 2014. Where were you working?" He was quiet so long the fluorescent light seemed to get louder. Then he sat down in the chair across from her, heavily, all at once, like a man giving up a wall he had been holding for a long time.
"Kestrel Point," he said. "I was the engineer on duty. The night of the storm." She did not move. "You knew my brother." "I knew Emeka." His voice was dry. "He was the best night man that station ever had. He could hear a bad splice through a wall." He turned a licorice drop over in his fingers and did not eat it. "I've known who you were since the day you applied. There was never a good way to say it, and then there was never any way at all."

They waited until the last researcher had gone and the library upstairs had dimmed to its night lights. Gus made tea on the hot plate, two chipped mugs, and set one in front of Nadia without asking, and she wrapped her hands around it.
"You want the whole of it," he said. "I do." He nodded slowly. "Then put your notebook away. This isn't a thing I can say twice."

"Then the phone rang. Not the emergency line. The office line, the one nobody had the number for. A man said there would be a weather log entry for the night. Storm damage, transmitter down, off the air from eight until morning. He said it would be in the book by the time we came in, and it was. He said we were good men and should stay good men."
"Did you report it?" The silence went on a long time. "I had a wife," Gus said at last. "A mortgage, a pension twelve years from the line. Emeka had a sister and a mother and a temper." He looked at her then, and his eyes were wet. "We made a bargain in that room. He would keep the tape and say nothing, and I would keep the log. And then the boat came in empty and your brother was gone, and I have kept my half of a bargain with a dead man for twelve years, and it has not bought me one night's sleep."

She went to North Pier on the Thursday night, after the archive closed and after she had eaten nothing and could not think of a reason not to. The fog had come in thick off the water, and the sodium lamps made soft yellow coins of themselves in the air.
North Pier was the oldest of the harbor's fingers and the least loved. The warehouses had their loading doors chained, and the whole length of it smelled of creosote and cold iron and the green rot of low tide. A fence carried a rendering of what the pier would become, glass towers, and the rain had got under the plastic and made the towers look as though they were weeping.

"Sorry. I didn't see you." "Nobody does." He had a thermos and a bucket with nothing in it. "Tomas Bel. I keep watch down here. Somebody has to, now that it's all going to be glass towers."
She introduced herself, and he looked at her the way old men do when deciding whether you are worth the trouble. "Okonkwo. You're the archivist, the one asking about the boat." "I'm looking for where it was found." "It's where you're standing." He nodded at the ring. "I helped catch her that morning. She came in slow, on the flood, no lights, and I said to the boy, that boat's been left."

Bellwether Hill sat above the city where the streets gave out and the pines began, and the rain met the roof of the care home in a steady, expensive hush. Nadia signed the visitor book with her real name, because false ones never held, and wrote "historical society" in the line for relationship, which was true enough.
The room smelled of antiseptic and boiled carrots and something older underneath, lavender maybe, or the ghost of it. Arthur Rusk sat by the window in a cardigan the color of oatmeal, a blanket squared over his knees, and he did not turn when she came in. Fluorescent light lay flat on the sill. Beyond the glass, a cedar shook in the wind.

She asked him about the Anselm. She asked him about the Pelargic. He hummed, and the humming had a tune to it, an old song, and he watched the rain as though it were a program he had seen before.
Then he turned and looked at her with terrifying clarity. "You're the girl," he said. "The one that came after. He said there was a girl who listened." "Who said?"

The invoice was at the bottom of the fourth box, folded twice and soft at the creases from years of being carried in a pocket. Ward Marine Electronics, Cape Verity. A VHF repair, an antenna mount, a depth sounder that had needed a new transducer. Cormac Doyle's name in the customer line, dated the spring of 2017 — three years after the Pelargic was found empty and her brother was declared drowned.
On the back, in pencil, in handwriting she had last seen on a reel label in a biscuit tin: "Ask for Eli. He knows the boat."

She knew him before he turned. She knew him by the set of his shoulders and the way he held the iron, delicate as a pen, and by the small habit of tilting his head to hear the set he was working on, as though the radio were speaking to him and not the other way around.
Then he turned.

The float was on the porch when she got home, sitting on the top step beside the mat with the rain beading on it. Green glass, the size of a grapefruit, wrapped in a cradle of knotted netting that had gone stiff with salt. She stopped with her key in the door and looked at it for a long time before she picked it up.
There was a note folded under the netting, damp at one corner, in pencil on a page torn from a pocket notebook. It said: "I am here. Come quietly." And beneath that, in the same careful hand: "Cinder Yards. Friday. 11:40."

Nobody else knew that. Not her mother. Not Fiona. Not Gus. It was a language with two speakers, and one of them had been dead for twelve years, and now the float sat in her hand on a wet autumn evening and the language was alive again.
She carried it inside and set it on the kitchen table under the light, and turned it, and watched the green deepen and thin where the glass was thick. Salt was crusted in the knots of the netting. There was a smear of engine grease on one side, as though it had been carried in a toolbox.

Nadia parked the Volvo where the access road gave out, at a chain-link gate whose padlock had been cut and hung back on its hasp. Rain ticked on the hood. Beyond the fence the Cinder Yards opened out in the last gray light, forty acres of rusted rails and dead locomotives, weeds shouldering up through the ballast like something refusing to be done with the world.
She had come early, the way she came early to everything. The field notebook was in her coat pocket; the laptop and the digitized tape were in the canvas bag beside her. Three weeks ago she had been a woman who cataloged other people's sounds. Then the green glass float had appeared on her porch, and the ordered basement of her life had cracked open.

"But you didn't." "No." He looked at his hands, at the grease under the nails. "I recorded it. Then I called Cormac, because Cormac knew the water and I didn't know who else to trust. He came down at one in the morning and listened twice. Then he asked me whether I wanted to be a witness for the next twenty years, or a man who was already dead."
The plan had been Cormac's. He took the Pelargic out himself and left her running in the shipping lane where she would be found. Emeka went over the side into a skiff moored at the cannery. By dawn the Pelargic was drifting empty and Elias Ward was already on the coast road north. Cormac told them the boy had gone out with him and fallen. He cried when he said it. Emeka thought he meant it.

"Mama stopped saying your name. Twelve years. You gave her a funeral with no body in it and you didn't even stay." "I stood at the back. Behind everybody." He kept his eyes on the rails. "I heard the priest. I heard her not crying."
The anger came up through her like tide water, and under it something else, warm and unbearable, that she could not yet name. She wanted to hit him again. She wanted never to let go of his sleeve. Both were true at once, so she sat with them and let the rain fill the silence.

The hospice was low and brick, set back from the Bellwether Hill road behind a stand of wind-bent pines. Nadia signed the register and waited under a fluorescent panel that hummed at a pitch she could feel in her teeth. The nurse told her Vera Lindqvist had been asking for her since morning.
Room six smelled of antiseptic and rain. Vera lay propped against the pillows, small as a child under the blanket, an oxygen line under her nose. Her hands were folded on the sheet, spotted and still. On the windowsill, where she could see it, sat the green glass float, holding the gray daylight and giving a little of it back.

"There was money," Nadia said. "For his family." "Through a lawyer in the city. Quiet, no admission of anything. Arthur called it a kindness." Vera's mouth thinned. "It was a price. The mother took it because she had two other children and no husband. I signed the paper that made it legal, and I have never once written my name without thinking of it."
"And the third of March?" Vera was quiet long enough that Nadia checked the red light. "Arthur called me at home that night, from his house on the hill. He said the station was going to put something on the air that shouldn't go out, and it needed to stay off. I wrote storm damage in the log myself. I put the pen down and my hand was steady, and that frightened me more than anything."

Nadia asked the only question left. "Why now?" "Because I'm dying, and I would like to stop being the woman who did those things. And because Arthur's son is tearing down the point and putting up glass towers, and after the ground is turned nobody will ask me anything again." She looked at the float. "Take that when I'm gone. It was my mother's."
"Can you say the last part again for the tape? About Arthur's order." Vera did, slower, in a voice going thin at the edges: the call, the order, the log, the inquiry buried, the money, the boy in the forepeak. The reels turned with a soft click, and under everything ran the hiss, that patient ocean sound Nadia had spent her whole working life listening past.

By four the rain had settled into a steady gray drizzle, and the bell over the door of Ward Marine Electronics rang once when Nadia came in. Emeka turned the sign to Closed and pulled the blind down over the glass. The shop smelled of solder and cold coffee and varnish.
He led her past benches of half-dismantled radios to the back room and moved the shelf of parts bins aside. In the wall behind it he had cut a panel, and in the cavity sat a steel cash box with a padlock. He worked the key and lifted out a cardboard sleeve.

Then the storm. The receiver opened on a wash of static and a man's voice came through in pieces: the Anselm, taking water, position given twice, a name. Tobias Renn. The archive dub had given them nine seconds of him. Here he lasted almost two minutes, calm and then not calm, saying they were going down and asking somebody to call his mother, and then the carrier closed over him like water.
After that, a click and a line hiss. Emeka had held the telephone receiver against the microphone. Arthur Rusk's voice was dry, unhurried, certain of being obeyed. "Put it down, Okonkwo. This channel is closed. You will not repeat what you heard tonight. Log it as storm damage and stay off the air until I say otherwise." Then Emeka's own voice, younger, saying, "Yes, sir," and the click of the line going dead.

Nadia sat back. Her hands were cold. "This is not a copy of a copy," she said. "It's continuous. Slate at the head, tone at the tail, the phone call in the middle. With Vera's confession, it's enough." Emeka nodded slowly. "Then we take it to your detective."
Her phone rang on the bench. Fiona, out of breath. "It's on the planning portal. Rusk Marine pulled the demolition forward. Kestrel Point comes down at first light. There's a crew staging at the Narrows now." Nadia put it on speaker so Emeka could hear. "That's the transmitter," she said. "That's the last of the station that isn't already rust."

The storm came in from the southwest all afternoon, and by nine the rain was going sideways against the archive windows and the radio was reading out closures in a flat, unhurried voice. Nadia stood in the basement doorway with her coat already on and listened to the coast road being taken away, mile by mile, the way the tide takes a beach.
They met in the lot behind the library. Fiona drove, because Fiona did not argue with weather. Gus came out of the side door with a canvas tool bag and a thermos and his boots laced tight, sixty-one years old and moving like a man who had somewhere to be. Serrano arrived last, in a raincoat too new for the season.

They parked a quarter mile short and walked the rest, hoods up, flashlights low. Gus led, because he had walked that ground for nine years and his feet remembered it even if his knees did not.
The door was not locked, which was its own kind of insult. Inside, the air smelled of mildew and old cigarettes and, beneath that, ozone, the ghost of a thousand small electricals. Their beams found a counter, a chair, a wall of grey steel cabinets.

She put it in the canvas bag, then touched her coat pocket, where the master reel sat wrapped in a sock and the small recorder held Vera's voice. The reel taken from her office had been Doyle's copy. This one had not left her brother's hands in twelve years.
Then the work lamp the crew had strung in the corridor died. Out in the yard the trailer's generator stopped, and its hum had been there so long she had stopped hearing it, and the dark came in like water. Gus made a sound that was almost relief. "Standby set," he said. "There's a diesel in the lean-to. Bring the torch."

The clock on the transmitter-room wall had stopped at 11:40 sometime in 2014 and nobody had ever wound it. Nadia looked at it while the valves warmed, and then she pulled the microphone over and said her name. "This is Nadia Okonkwo, archivist at the Marrow Bay Municipal Archive. What follows was recorded in this room on the third of March, 2014."
She cued the master reel and let it run. The hiss came first, the old sea-sound of quarter-inch tape, and under the hiss the storm that had stood over the coast for three days. Then the carrier. Then a voice from a ship that had already sunk in the records, calling for help it would not get. Then a man's voice, flat and unhurried, telling someone to put it down. Then her brother, whispering her name, telling her not to look for him but to look at the water.

Headlights turned off the point road and came up the track and stopped beside the excavator. A car door. Then Desmond Rusk was walking the last of the mud with no umbrella, his coat dark to the shoulder, his shoes ruined, and she understood that he had come out early to see the site before the crew and had heard the radio instead.
He stood in the doorway with the rain running off him and looked at the microphone and then at her. "Turn it off," he said. His voice was quiet. He was not the man from the corridor at Bellwether Hill; he had lost the umbrella and the talk about weather. "You don't understand what you're doing. My father is a sick old man. There are families in this town who have lived with this for twelve years. You think you're helping them?"

"Our family lived with it too," Nadia said, and turned back to the board.
Serrano came across the room with his coat open and his badge already out, and his voice was flat and tired and certain. He told Rusk he was under arrest, and he named the things plainly: tampering with evidence, obstruction, conspiracy. He said the words a police officer says, and Rusk did not resist him, and did not look at any of them again.

The archive was cold by December. Nadia wore fingerless gloves to splice, and the radiator clanked twice an hour and gave up, and the fluorescent tubes over the workbench hummed in a key she had never been able to name. She had always liked the winter down there, the whole building settling above her head. Vera's green float stood on the windowsill above the workbench, holding the gray light.
The register was a ledger the size of a suitcase door, bound in red buckram, with columns ruled in 1961 by a librarian whose handwriting had never been improved on. In October she had left a line blank in it, carried the tape home instead, and lied by omission to the one institution she believed in. Now she opened the ledger at the back and took up a pencil and filled the line in.

She played it through once at quarter speed for the catalog notes, the way she would have done in October if she had been honest. At quarter speed the storm became a room, and the voices became structures, and the hiss became what it had always been: the tape itself, the oxide and the binder and the long fall of a signal into air. She listened for an hour with the headphones on and heard nothing new. She listened again the next day, and there was still nothing in it but weather and men and the sea.
On the Sunday before Christmas she drove Emeka out to Salt Row. He sat in the passenger seat with his hands on his knees and did not talk, and the tape deck was still broken, and the heater clicked and roared. The house looked small under the wet sky, the paint grey with salt, the porch light on although it was afternoon.

Rusk Marine Holdings took its name off the trailer at Kestrel Point in January. The station was fenced and listed for survey, the mast standing, the transmitter room sealed with a padlock and a notice that said nothing about the log inside it.
Serrano called her twice that winter, each time with less in his voice than the time before, and the second time he said the county had charged Desmond Rusk with three counts and that Arthur Rusk had died at Bellwether Hill on a Tuesday without ever being asked a question in a room with a recorder in it.
